title: CSC3710 2026-10-20: Context-Free Grammars, Derivations, and Regular Grammars

questions.q: A context-free grammar is a quadruple G = (N, Σ, P, S). What is Σ?
choices: A finite set of terminal symbols (the alphabet)
A finite set of non-terminal symbols (variables)
questions.explain: N is the set of non-terminals (variables), P is the set of rules, and S ∈ N is the start symbol. Σ is the alphabet of terminal symbols.

questions.q: In G = (N, Σ, P, S), which statement about S is correct?
choices: S is a special non-terminal: S ∈ N
S is a terminal: S ∈ Σ
S is one of the rules in P
S is the set of all sentences of the grammar
questions.explain: The start symbol is a special non-terminal. Every derivation of a sentence in L(G) begins with it.

questions.q: In a context-free grammar, the same symbol may be used both as a terminal and as a non-terminal.
questions.explain: The definition requires N ∩ Σ = ∅. Terminals and non-terminals must be different symbols.

questions.q: In a context-free grammar rule u → w, what can u be?
choices: Any string of terminals and non-terminals
questions.explain: The left-hand side of a CFG rule is a single non-terminal. The right-hand side w can be any string over N ∪ Σ, including λ.

questions.q: In a context-free grammar rule u → w, the right-hand side w may be λ, the empty string.
questions.explain: w may be λ. A rule such as B → λ is called a λ-rule.

questions.q: Let N = {S, A} and Σ = {a, b}. Which of these are valid context-free grammar rules?
questions.explain: The left side must be exactly one non-terminal. aS, a, and SA are not single non-terminals. The right side can be any string over N ∪ Σ, including λ or AA.

questions.q: What does the notation A → x | y mean in a grammar?
choices: Two separate rules, A → x and A → y, written on one line
One rule whose right side is the set union of x and y
A rewrites to x only if y cannot be applied
A rewrites to x followed by y
questions.explain: The vertical bar is shorthand that puts several rules with the same left side on one line. It is not a set union.

questions.q: What is a rule whose right-hand side is λ called?
questions.explain: A rule like B → λ is a λ-rule because λ is on its right-hand side.

questions.q: The rule B → bB is called a 'B rule'. Why?
choices: B is on its left-hand side
B is the last symbol on its right-hand side
questions.explain: A u-rule is named after its left-hand side, the non-terminal it rewrites.

questions.q: In a grammar, what is a sentence?
choices: A derived string that contains only terminal symbols
Any string of terminals and non-terminals
A string that still contains at least one non-terminal
A single rule of the grammar
questions.explain: No rule can be applied to a sentence, so the derivation stops there. L(G) is the set of sentences derivable from the start symbol.

questions.q: Apply the rule S → aSbb once to the string aSb. What string do you get? (Write it with no spaces.)
questions.explain: Replace the S in aSb with aSbb: a + aSbb + b = aaSbbb.

questions.q: Apply the rule A → aAbb once to the string bbbAb. What string do you get? (Write it with no spaces.)
questions.explain: Replace the A with aAbb: bbb + aAbb + b = bbbaAbbb. A rule can be applied to any string that contains its left-hand-side variable.

questions.q: What does v ⇒* u mean?
choices: u can be obtained from v by zero or more rule applications
u can be obtained from v by exactly one rule application
u can be obtained from v by one or more rule applications
v → u is a rule of the grammar
questions.explain: The star means zero or more steps, so v ⇒* v always holds. A single ⇒ means one step.

questions.q: What does a number above the derivation arrow mean, as in v ⇒⁴ u?
choices: u is obtained from v in exactly 4 rule applications
u is obtained from v in at most 4 rule applications
u is 4 symbols longer than v
Rule number 4 is applied to v
questions.explain: A number above ⇒ gives the exact number of derivation steps.

questions.q: What is the difference between A → aA and aAB ⇒ aaAB?
choices: A → aA is a rule in P; aAB ⇒ aaAB is a derivation step that applies that rule to a string
They mean exactly the same thing
A → aA is a derivation step; aAB ⇒ aaAB is a rule
→ means logical implication and ⇒ means concatenation
questions.explain: → appears inside a rule. ⇒ shows one rule being applied to a string. Neither one means logical implication.

questions.q: Under the recursive definition of derivability, every string v is derivable from itself.
questions.explain: This is the basis step: v is derivable from v using zero rule applications.

questions.q: In the recursive definition of the set of strings derivable from v, what does the closure condition say?
choices: A string is derivable from v only if it can be obtained from v by finitely many rule applications
Every string over N ∪ Σ is derivable from v
If xAy is derivable from v and A → w is a rule, then xwy is derivable from v
questions.explain: The third choice is the basis and the fourth is the recursive step. Closure says nothing else is derivable.

questions.q: The grammar notation ⇒* (zero or more derivation steps) corresponds to which notation for automata?
choices: ⊢* (zero or more transitions between machine configurations)
questions.explain: For machines, ⊢ is one transition between configurations and ⊢* is zero or more. ⇒ and ⇒* are the grammar versions.

questions.q: Every string in L(G) has exactly one sequence of rule applications that derives it from the start symbol.
questions.explain: Derivations need not be unique. In S → aSb | aSbb | λ, the string aaSbbb is reached by applying rule 1 then rule 2, or rule 2 then rule 1. This leads to the topic of ambiguity.

questions.q: What language does the grammar S → aSb | aSbb | λ generate?
questions.explain: Each a comes with one or two b's. If rule 1 is used i times and rule 2 is used j times, then n = i + j and m = i + 2j, so n ≤ m ≤ 2n.

questions.q: Which strings are generated by S → aSb | aSbb | λ?
questions.explain: Generated strings are aⁿbᵐ with n ≤ m ≤ 2n. aaabb has too few b's (needs at least 3), aabbbbb has too many (at most 4), and abab does not have all a's before all b's.

questions.q: How many sentences of length at most 4 does S → aSb | aSbb | λ generate?
questions.explain: They are λ, ab, abb, and aabb.

questions.q: In the language of S → aSb | aSbb | λ, how many different sentences have exactly 3 a's?
questions.explain: With n = 3, m ranges from 3 to 6: aaabbb, aaabbbb, aaabbbbb, aaabbbbbb.

questions.q: { aⁿbᵐ | n ≥ 0, 0 < m ≤ 2n } correctly describes the language of S → aSb | aSbb | λ.
questions.explain: The lower bound on m must be n, not 0. This version wrongly allows strings like aaab and wrongly excludes λ.

questions.q: Why does the language of S → aSb | aSbb | λ use the condition n ≥ 0 rather than n ≥ 1?
choices: Because λ is in the language: S ⇒ λ gives n = m = 0
Because the rule S → aSb always adds at least one a
Because every derivation must use S → aSbb at least once
Because exponents in set notation can never start at 1
questions.explain: Applying S → λ immediately derives the empty string, so zero a's must be allowed.

questions.q: When building a derivation tree level by level, if the same string appears on two branches, you only need to expand one of them.
questions.explain: Identical strings have identical subtrees, so a repeat adds no new sentences and can be dropped.

questions.q: Consider the grammar ⟨dedication⟩ → ⟨parents⟩, ⟨parents⟩ → ⟨firstname⟩⟨lastname⟩, ⟨firstname⟩ → Donald | Mary, ⟨lastname⟩ → Sue, with start symbol ⟨dedication⟩. What is its set of terminal symbols Σ?
questions.explain: The bracketed names are non-terminals. Donald, Mary, and Sue never appear on the left of a rule, so they are terminals.

questions.q: Consider the grammar ⟨dedication⟩ → ⟨parents⟩, ⟨parents⟩ → ⟨firstname⟩⟨lastname⟩, ⟨firstname⟩ → Donald | Mary, ⟨lastname⟩ → Sue, with start symbol ⟨dedication⟩. How many sentences are in its language?
questions.explain: L(G) = { Donald Sue, Mary Sue }. The only choice in any derivation is which ⟨firstname⟩ rule to use.

questions.q: Consider the grammar S → aSa | aBa, B → bB | b, with start symbol S. What is the shortest string it generates?
questions.explain: S ⇒ aBa ⇒ aba, using S → aBa and then B → b.

questions.q: What language does S → aSa | aBa, B → bB | b (start symbol S) generate?
questions.explain: Both S rules add one a on each side, so the counts match. S → aBa guarantees n ≥ 1, and B produces one or more b's.

questions.q: What language does S → abScd | λ generate?
questions.explain: Each use of rule 1 adds one ab on the left and one cd on the right, for example S ⇒ abScd ⇒ ababScdcd. Parentheses are needed to repeat a block.

questions.q: What is the shortest string in { a bⁿ c dⁿ | n ≥ 0 }?
questions.explain: With n = 0, b and d disappear, but a and c are not affected by the exponent.

questions.q: Which string belongs to { a bⁿ c dⁿ | n ≥ 0 }?
questions.explain: abbcdd is the n = 2 case. The exponent applies only to b and to d, so a and c each appear exactly once.

questions.q: In { a bⁿ c dⁿ | n ≥ 0 }, each exponent n applies only to the single symbol directly before it (b or d), not to a or c.
questions.explain: An exponent binds to one symbol, just as in arithmetic. To repeat a block such as ab, you must write (ab)ⁿ.

questions.q: What is the shortest string in { (ab)ⁿ(cd)ⁿ | n ≥ 0 }?
questions.explain: With n = 0 both blocks disappear, which leaves λ.

questions.q: What is the shortest string in { aⁿ bᵐ cᵐ d²ⁿ | n ≥ 0, m > 0 }?
questions.explain: Use the minimum exponents: n = 0 and m = 1.

questions.q: Which grammar generates { aⁿ bᵐ cᵐ d²ⁿ | n ≥ 0, m > 0 }?
choices: S → aSdd | A,   A → bAc | bc
S → aSd | A,   A → bAc | bc
S → aSdd | A,   A → bAc | λ
S → aaSd | A,   A → bAc | bc
questions.explain: Each a must be matched by two d's, and the middle needs at least one b...c pair. The second grammar gives one d per a, the third allows m = 0, and the fourth gives two a's per d.

questions.q: What language does S → aSbb | λ generate?
questions.explain: Each use of S → aSbb adds one a and exactly two b's.

questions.q: Every language has exactly one correct way to be written in set-builder notation.
questions.explain: The same set can often be written in several correct ways. For example, a⁺b* = aa*b* = { aⁿbᵐ | n ≥ 1, m ≥ 0 }.

questions.q: Every regular language is a context-free language.
questions.explain: Regular languages are a subset of context-free languages, which are a subset of all languages P(Σ*).

questions.q: Every context-free language is a regular language.
questions.explain: The converse fails. For example, { aⁱbⁱ | i ≥ 0 } is context-free but not regular.

questions.q: { aⁱbⁱ | i ≥ 0 } is context-free but not regular.
questions.explain: A context-free grammar generates it (S → aSb | λ). Showing that it is not regular takes a proof.

questions.q: Where does { aⁿbᵐ | n ≥ 0, n ≤ m ≤ 2n } sit in the language hierarchy?
choices: Nowhere: an infinite set of strings is not a language
questions.explain: S → aSb | aSbb | λ generates it, so it is context-free. It is not regular, though proving that takes a separate argument.

questions.q: Which formalism can generate context-free languages that are not regular?
questions.explain: DFAs, regular expressions, and regular grammars all describe only regular languages. Context-free grammars generate context-free languages.

questions.q: If a language is generated by a grammar that is not a regular grammar, that proves the language is not regular.
questions.explain: A non-regular grammar can still generate a regular language. G1 (S → AB, A → aA | a, B → bB | λ) is not a regular grammar, yet it generates a⁺b*. Showing that a language is not regular requires a proof.

questions.q: What does P(Σ*) denote?
choices: The set of all languages over Σ, including the empty language
The set of all strings over Σ
The set of all context-free languages over Σ
The set of all grammars over Σ
questions.explain: Σ* is the set of all strings. A language is a subset of Σ*, so the power set P(Σ*) is the set of all languages.

questions.q: What language does the grammar S → AB, A → aA | a, B → bB | λ generate?
questions.explain: A produces one or more a's (A → aA repeats, A → a ends). B produces zero or more b's (B → bB repeats, B → λ ends).

questions.q: What is the shortest sentence generated by S → AB, A → aA | a, B → bB | λ?
questions.explain: S ⇒ AB ⇒ aB ⇒ a, using S → AB, then A → a, then B → λ.

questions.q: For the grammar S → aS | aA, A → bA | λ, which derivation produces the shortest sentence?
questions.explain: There are no rules S → bA or S → λ. A → bA is an A rule, so it cannot be applied to S. The shortest path is S → aA followed by A → λ.

questions.q: What language does the grammar S → aS | aA, A → bA | λ generate?
questions.explain: S → aS piles up a's, S → aA adds one final a and switches to A, A → bA adds b's, and A → λ finishes.

questions.q: Two grammars with different rules and different numbers of non-terminals can generate exactly the same language.
questions.explain: S → AB, A → aA | a, B → bB | λ (3 non-terminals, 5 rules) and S → aS | aA, A → bA | λ (2 non-terminals, 4 rules) both generate a⁺b*.

questions.q: In the grammar S → AB, A → aA | a, B → bB | λ, once S → AB has been applied, S never appears again in the derivation.
questions.explain: No rule has S on its right side. After the first step, only A rules and B rules apply, in any order.

questions.q: A regular grammar is a context-free grammar in which every rule has an allowed form. Which forms are allowed? (A, B are non-terminals; a is a terminal.)
questions.explain: The allowed forms are a single terminal, a terminal followed by one non-terminal, or λ.

questions.q: Which rule keeps the grammar S → AB, A → aA | a, B → bB | λ from being a regular grammar?
questions.explain: Its right side is two non-terminals concatenated, which matches none of A → a, A → aB, or A → λ. All the other rules have an allowed form.

questions.q: The grammar S → aS | aA, A → bA | λ is a regular grammar.
questions.explain: S → aS, S → aA, and A → bA have the form A → aB, and A → λ is a λ-rule.

questions.q: A grammar that is not a regular grammar can still generate a regular language.
questions.explain: S → AB, A → aA | a, B → bB | λ is not regular but generates a⁺b*. Because that language is regular, a regular grammar for it also exists.

questions.q: Every regular grammar generates a regular language.
questions.explain: Regular grammars generate regular languages. In the other direction, every regular language has a regular grammar.

questions.q: In the regular-grammar form A → aB, the non-terminal B is allowed to be A itself, as in A → aA.
questions.explain: B can be any non-terminal, including A. Rules such as S → aS are allowed.

questions.q: Which of these is a regular grammar (rules only of the forms A → a, A → aB, A → λ) that generates a*b?
choices: S → AB,  A → aA | λ,  B → b
questions.explain: S → aS | b gives zero or more a's followed by one b, and both rules have allowed forms. S → Sa | b generates ba*. S → aSb | λ generates aⁿbⁿ. The last grammar generates a*b, but S → AB is not an allowed form.

questions.q: In the grammar S → aSa | aBa, B → bB | b, which rules violate the regular-grammar forms?
questions.explain: A terminal after the non-terminal is not allowed, so aSa and aBa break the form. B → bB has the form A → aB, and B → b has the form A → a.
